title: Cautions
hookLine: teachers warn against magic, charms sold for money, and study without grounding

lines: A CHARM WITH A PRICE TAG.
cards: A charm in a shop window, with Hebrew letters stamped on it and a little card promising luck. A course online that says it will unlock the secret names in a weekend, card details please.
The word Kabbalah can end up on a price tag. But some of the sharpest warnings about this kind of thing don't come from critics outside.
They come from inside the tradition, from the Torah, the Mishnah and its own teachers.

teach.b: Cautions. First, the Torah's own line. Deuteronomy names practices that are not to be found among the people: divining, reading omens, sorcery, casting spells, asking the dead.
Then it sums up what it wants instead, in a short phrase that begins tamim tihyeh: be whole-hearted with the LORD your God. Not clever, not powerful. Whole.

teach.h: NOT A CROWN, NOT A SPADE.
teach.b: Second, the crown and the spade. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Tzadok says not to make the Torah a crown to make yourself great, nor a spade to dig with. Holy learning isn't a tool for status or a way to dig up money.
Charms sold for profit fall right under that warning. Third, words as cures.
Maimonides objected to people who whisper over a wound and read a verse of Torah to heal it. The words of Torah, he wrote, are healing for the soul, not medicine for the body.
And within Kabbalah itself, teachers drew a line between learning about God and trying to use holy names to change things in the world, and warned students away from the second. Fourth, grounding.
Mystical ideas without a floor under them can drift: into fear, into pride, into the feeling of having secret knowledge others don't.
The tradition's answer is a floor of plain learning, a community, and a teacher whose life matches their words.
So study carefully looks like ordinary questions. Who taught this person? What do they ask of me?
Does this teaching send me back toward kindness, honest work and the commandments, or toward my wallet? A careful student isn't a suspicious one. They just check the ground before they stand on it.

how: Jewish mysticism is traditionally studied within a framework of Torah, Jewish law and community, and teachers in the tradition warn students away from amulets, paid blessings and the use of holy names as magic.

he objected: the Torah's words heal the soul, not the body.

games.q: a shop offers a charm stamped with Hebrew letters, said to bring luck, for a price. what do the tradition's teachers warn?
o: buy it: holy letters work anywhere.
be careful: holy words aren't tools for magic or for sale.
Hebrew letters mean nothing at all.
games.why: the Torah forbids spells and omens, Avot warns against using Torah as a spade, and Maimonides objected to verses used as cures.

practice: Bring to mind something you've picked up lately about faith or about yourself, a post, a video, a piece of advice, and hold it up to the light: where did it come from, and did it ask you for money, or fear, or nothing at all?
Then bring to mind one source you trust more deeply, a teacher, a book, a person whose life matches their words, and rest with them.

wordCard.voice: Cautions. The tradition's own warnings: no magic, no selling holy things, and no mystical study without solid ground beneath it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: study carefully. Holy learning is not a crown and not a spade. See you tomorrow.
